pages.content:
Website information

Privacy Policy

How information sent through IanProject’s communication channels is handled.

Information You Choose to Send

IanProject may receive information that you voluntarily send by email, WhatsApp or other linked communication channels. This may include your name, company, contact details, project location, drawings, product lists, quantities, specifications and reference images.

How Information Is Used

Information is used to respond to enquiries, review project requirements, prepare quotations, coordinate samples or production, provide delivery support and maintain relevant business records.

Service Providers and Project Partners

Relevant project information may be shared with suitable suppliers, logistics providers or professional service providers when needed to review or fulfil your request. Information is limited to what is reasonably required for that purpose.

Third-Party Platforms

This website links to email, WhatsApp, YouTube and social-media platforms. Their own privacy terms apply when you use those services. IanProject does not control third-party websites or applications.

Website Analytics

IanProject uses Google Analytics to understand website traffic and improve site content. Google Analytics may collect information such as pages visited, approximate location, device and browser information, referral source and interactions with the website using cookies or similar technologies. This information is reviewed in aggregated reports and is not used by IanProject to identify visitors personally. You can restrict analytics cookies through your browser settings. Google processes analytics information under its own privacy terms.

Retention and Security

Information is retained only as reasonably needed for enquiries, project coordination, legal obligations and business records. Reasonable measures are used to protect information, but no internet transmission or storage system can be guaranteed completely secure.

Your Request

You may ask about, correct or request deletion of information you have provided, subject to applicable record-keeping requirements. Contact info@ianproject.com.

Policy Updates

This policy may be updated when website features or business processes change. Last updated: August 2026.

posts.title: Cabinet Board Environmental Grades Explained
posts.description: A clear guide to ENF, E0, E1, F★★★★, EU REACH, CARB Phase 2, TSCA Title VI, NAF and ULEF for cabinet boards.
posts.content:
Cabinet material guide

What ENF, E0, E1, F★★★★, CARB, NAF and other familiar labels really mean.

​Updated August 24, 2026 · 9-minute read

As society develops, environmental damage has become increasingly serious. People are gradually becoming more environmentally conscious, and expectations for healthier materials in home decoration continue to rise.

When buying custom furniture, we often hear suppliers say, “Our boards are E1 or E0,” or show labels such as “F grade.” Others emphasise that their products are “formaldehyde-free.” But what do these terms actually mean? Most buyers have only a vague understanding and may not know what each grade represents.

In this guide, we reveal what cabinet board environmental grades really mean.

Formaldehyde-emission standards at a glance

The table is arranged from lower numerical chamber limits to broader market-specific systems. Values can be compared only when the test method and unit are the same.

Do not directly rank mg/m³, mg/L and ppm values. Different standards use different chambers, specimens, conditioning procedures and calculations.

China

ENF: ≤ 0.025 mg/m³

ENF is the strictest grade in China’s GB/T 39600-2021 classification. It is commonly selected for projects seeking a lower-emission specification, including high-density whole-house cabinetry.

Because the limit is measured under the standard’s controlled chamber conditions, ENF should be written into the material schedule together with the board manufacturer, production mill, substrate and thickness. A general brochure or a certificate for another panel is not sufficient.

ENF does not mean absolute zero formaldehyde. Wood naturally contains trace formaldehyde, and a completed room can contain emissions from flooring, paint, adhesives and other furnishings. The practical benefit is a stricter panel-emission target within the Chinese grading system.

Best used when: a project contains extensive cabinetry, seeks a lower-emission specification, serves sensitive occupants or has sufficient budget for a higher board grade.

China and other markets

E0: ≤ 0.050 mg/m³ under the Chinese standard

E0 is the middle grade in GB/T 39600-2021 and offers a practical balance between emission performance and cost for many residential cabinet projects. It is stricter than China’s mandatory E1 baseline but more widely attainable than ENF.

The term E0 also appears outside China, but it has no universal global definition. Some suppliers use E0 as a commercial description based on a different national standard or test method. The supplier should therefore state the standard number, unit and measured result rather than provide only an “E0” label.

For a cabinet quotation, specify whether E0 applies only to the carcass board or also to doors, back panels, drawer bottoms and other wood-based components. A project can lose the intended benefit when secondary panels are substituted with an unverified grade.

Best used when: a residential project wants a meaningful improvement over the baseline while maintaining a balanced material budget.

China and international specifications

E1: ≤ 0.124 mg/m³ under the Chinese standard

GB 18580-2017 sets E1 as China’s mandatory baseline for indoor wood-based panels. A compliant E1 board is not automatically unsafe; it meets the applicable Chinese limit when properly tested.

E1 terminology is also used internationally, so the cited standard and method must be checked. European E1 references and Chinese E1 results can look similar in name without being interchangeable in every procurement document. The letters alone do not prove that two products were tested under identical conditions.

For cost-controlled projects, E1 may be an acceptable starting point when the report is valid and the design also limits total panel area, seals exposed edges, controls adhesives and provides ventilation. Buyers should not accept an expired report or a report issued for a different mill.

Best used when: the project requires a compliant baseline and manages the whole-room material load rather than evaluating one board in isolation.

China sources: GB 18580-2017 and GB/T 39600-2021.

Japan

F★★★★: Japan’s highest F-star classification

F★★★★ is the highest formaldehyde-emission classification within relevant Japanese JIS and JAS systems and is widely recognised in Japanese building-material and furniture supply chains. Lower star classifications can be subject to tighter restrictions on the area permitted for interior use.

Japanese values are commonly expressed in mg/L using a desiccator method. Do not directly convert them into Chinese chamber results or assume that a visually similar number is equivalent. The product category and referenced JIS or JAS standard determine the applicable test and acceptance criteria.

When a supplier claims F★★★★, request the certificate or registration information, product name, manufacturing site and scope. Confirm that certification covers the panel being supplied rather than only imported raw material or another collection.

Best used when: the destination is Japan or the project specification explicitly requires certified Japanese F-star materials.

Source: Japanese Agricultural Standards.

European Union

EU REACH: ≤ 0.062 mg/m³

Commission Regulation (EU) 2023/1464 introduces a formaldehyde-emission restriction for furniture and wood-based articles placed on the EU market. The limit applies under specified chamber conditions from 6 August 2026.

EU REACH is a legal article requirement, not another E-grade. It addresses emissions from the article placed on the market, so a raw-board certificate alone may not fully demonstrate that a completed cabinet is compliant.

EU-bound buyers should define responsibility for testing, technical documentation and supplier declarations in the purchase contract. Edge banding, laminates, adhesives, backs and other components should remain consistent with the evaluated construction.

Best used when: furniture or wood-based articles will be placed on the European Union market after the restriction becomes applicable.

Source: Commission Regulation (EU) 2023/1464.

California and the United States

CARB Phase 2 and TSCA Title VI

US requirements use different maximum limits by panel type: 0.05 ppm for hardwood plywood, 0.09 ppm for particleboard, 0.11 ppm for MDF and 0.13 ppm for thin MDF. A single “CARB value” is therefore incomplete unless the panel type is identified.

CARB Phase 2 applies through California’s programme, while TSCA Title VI is the US federal requirement. Covered panels are linked to third-party certification, quality-control testing, recordkeeping and labelling obligations.

For finished cabinets, request the panel manufacturer and mill, third-party certifier, product type and compliance statement. The cabinet factory’s own company certificate does not replace traceability to compliant composite wood panels.

Best used when: cabinets or regulated composite wood components are manufactured for sale, supply or import into the United States.

Sources: US EPA and California Air Resources Board.

United States and international claims

NAF and ULEF

NAF means no-added-formaldehyde-based resin. ULEF means ultra-low-emitting-formaldehyde resin. They describe resin systems and regulatory qualification pathways rather than ordinary positions on a universal grade scale.

NAF does not mean absolute zero formaldehyde because wood naturally contains trace amounts. ULEF also should not be interpreted as one fixed emission number without the applicable approval conditions.

Approvals and exemptions are normally specific to a manufacturer, mill and product. Request current documentation and check whether ongoing production-control requirements remain satisfied. Marketing phrases such as “aldehyde-free” should never replace the regulatory evidence.

Best used when: the project specifically requires no-added-formaldehyde resin or an approved ultra-low-emitting resin system and the supplier can provide traceable documentation.

Buying recommendations

  • ENF: consider for homes with babies, pregnant occupants, older people or sensitive users, high-density whole-house cabinetry, or when the budget supports a lower-emission specification.
  • E0: a cost-effective choice that meets the environmental expectations of many general residential projects.
  • E1: meets China’s basic compliant limit. Confirm the report and manage total cabinet volume, exposed edges, adhesives and ventilation.

A board grade alone cannot guarantee indoor-air quality. Final room concentration also depends on material quantity, flooring, paint, adhesives, temperature, humidity and ventilation.

Tell IanProject your destination country, cabinet drawings, board specification and target price. We can help organise the material requirements and match them to a suitable cabinet manufacturing solution.

posts.title: Cabinet Board Types Explained
posts.description: Compare plywood, particleboard, MDF, solid wood, OSB, eco-board and moisture-resistant cabinet boards by structure, performance and application.
posts.content:
Cabinet material guide

Plywood, particleboard, MDF, solid wood, OSB, eco-board and green-core moisture-resistant board compared by structure, performance, finish and best application.

​Updated August 25, 2026 · 12-minute read

When choosing kitchen cabinets, buyers often focus first on the colour and door style. However, the material hidden beneath the surface has a major influence on cabinet stability, moisture resistance, machining, weight, price and service life.

Plywood, particleboard and MDF are not simply “good, better and best.” Each material has a different structure and is suitable for different parts of a cabinet. A well-designed project may use one board for the carcass and another for painted or shaped doors.

This guide explains how the main cabinet board types differ and how to select the right combination for your project.

First understand the board structure

  1. Surface layer: the visible finish, such as melamine, wood veneer, lacquer, PET, PVC or HPL.
  2. Core layer: the substrate that provides most of the panel’s structure, such as plywood, particleboard or MDF.
  3. Backing layer: a balancing layer that helps the panel remain flat and stable.

Do not confuse the substrate with the finish. “Melamine cabinet” usually describes a melamine-faced board; the core underneath may be particleboard, MDF or plywood.

Cabinet board types compared

1. Plywood: strong and stable for demanding areas

Plywood is manufactured from thin wood veneers. Adjacent layers normally run in different grain directions, helping the panel resist movement and distribute loads more evenly than a single piece of solid wood.

For cabinetry, plywood is valued for good screw holding and practical moisture tolerance. It is frequently specified for sink cabinets, bathroom vanities, long shelves and premium carcasses. It is not automatically waterproof: performance depends on the wood species, veneer quality, adhesive system, face finish and edge sealing.

Learn More

2. Particleboard: practical and cost-effective

Particleboard is made from wood particles bonded with resin and pressed into a flat panel. Its uniform thickness and efficient use of wood resources make it one of the most common substrates for cabinet carcasses and ready-to-assemble furniture.

A well-made moisture-resistant particleboard with correctly sealed edges can perform reliably in normal kitchen use. Problems usually arise when unprotected edges are exposed to standing water or when unsuitable low-density boards are used around heavily loaded fittings.

Learn More

3. MDF: the preferred core for smooth and shaped doors

Medium-density fibreboard is produced from refined wood fibres mixed with resin and pressed into a dense, uniform panel. Because it has no visible chips or veneer layers, its faces and edges can be machined smoothly.

MDF is especially suitable for lacquered doors, routed profiles, grooves, curved details and PVC-wrapped fronts. Standard MDF should not be used where it may absorb water. Moisture-resistant MDF improves performance in humid environments, but exposed edges and drilled areas still need proper sealing.

Learn More

4. Solid wood: natural character for premium cabinet details

Solid wood is natural timber rather than a reconstituted panel. In cabinetry, it is commonly machined into door frames, rails, stiles, mouldings, trims and other visible components. Its grain, colour variation and ability to be refinished give it a premium, authentic appearance.

Wood naturally responds to changes in temperature and humidity. Good construction therefore uses properly dried timber, stable species, suitable joints and panel designs that allow controlled movement. Solid wood is not automatically the best material for every carcass: wide panels can expand, shrink, cup or warp if moisture content and construction are poorly controlled.

Learn More

5. OSB: structural strength with a distinctive strand texture

Oriented strand board is made from long, thin wood strands arranged in layers, bonded with resin and pressed under heat. The strands in adjoining layers are oriented in different directions to improve strength and dimensional performance.

OSB is widely used as a structural panel, but it is less common in conventional finished kitchen interiors because of its coarse surface and visible strands. It can be appropriate for industrial-style cabinetry, workshop storage, concealed structural components or project-specific designs when the selected grade, surface finish and edge protection meet the application.

Learn More

6. Eco-board: verify the core behind the marketing name

“Eco-board” is a common Chinese market term rather than one internationally standardised board type. It usually refers to a ready-finished panel with melamine decorative faces over a plywood or wood-strip core. Some suppliers use the same name for other substrates, so the label alone does not identify the structure.

Eco-board can be convenient for wardrobes, cabinet carcasses, shelves and interior furniture because the surface is already finished and requires no additional painting. Its stability, moisture resistance, screw holding and emission performance depend on the actual core material, adhesive, facing quality and edge sealing—not on the word “eco.”

Learn More

7. MR particleboard: practical moisture resistance for cabinet carcasses

Moisture-resistant particleboard is made from wood particles bonded with a resin system formulated to perform better than standard particleboard in humid conditions. Many manufacturers add green dye so it can be identified during production, but the colour itself is not a performance standard or proof of certification.

MR particleboard is commonly used for melamine-faced kitchen carcasses, bathroom vanities, laundry cabinets and projects in humid regions. It retains particleboard’s advantages—consistent thickness, efficient production and competitive cost—while offering improved resistance to intermittent humidity and accidental splashes.

It is moisture-resistant, not waterproof. Standing water, plumbing leaks and unsealed cut edges can still cause swelling. Edge banding, sink cut-outs, drilled holes and exposed backs must be protected correctly.

Learn More

8. MR MDF: moisture-resistant core for smooth and shaped doors

Moisture-resistant MDF is manufactured from fine wood fibres and a moisture-resistant resin formulation. Its cut edge is dense and uniform rather than visibly chipped, which distinguishes it from MR particleboard and makes it suitable for precise routing and smooth finishing.

MR MDF is often selected for lacquered doors, shaker profiles, grooves, PVC-wrapped fronts and other shaped components used in kitchens or humid interiors. It offers better humidity resistance than standard MDF while retaining the smooth faces and machinability required for decorative door production.

MR MDF is also not waterproof. Routed profiles, hinge holes, handle holes and exposed edges need a complete coating or sealing system. Buyers should verify the declared MR grade and test data rather than relying on the green colour alone.

Learn More

The surface finish still matters

The same substrate can perform and look very different after finishing. Melamine is durable and economical; lacquer provides a smooth premium appearance; natural veneer gives real wood grain; PET offers a uniform modern surface; and HPL is selected where higher wear resistance is important.

The finish, edge banding and back layer help protect the core, but they cannot turn an unsuitable substrate into a waterproof panel. Cabinet performance comes from the complete system: substrate, finish, adhesive, edge sealing, hardware fixing and installation conditions.

Selection recommendations

  • For a cost-effective standard kitchen: use quality moisture-resistant particleboard with melamine faces and well-sealed edges for the carcass.
  • For lacquered or shaped doors: use MDF because its fine, uniform core supports routing and smooth finishing.
  • For sink cabinets and moisture-prone areas: consider properly specified plywood or another verified moisture-resistant board, together with sealed edges and leak protection.
  • For premium all-plywood cabinetry: verify the veneer, glue, core gaps, surface finish and actual panel grade instead of relying only on the word “plywood.”
  • For natural premium doors and details: use properly dried solid wood with construction that allows normal movement as humidity changes.
  • For exposed industrial-style projects: OSB can create a distinctive appearance, but confirm the panel grade, surface preparation and edge protection.
  • For eco-board: do not accept the marketing name alone; specify whether the core is plywood, wood-strip board or another substrate and verify its test report.
  • For humid cabinet carcasses: choose verified MR particleboard and protect every cut edge; green colour alone is not proof of performance.
  • For shaped doors in humid interiors: choose MR MDF with a complete coating and edge-sealing system.
  • For export projects: confirm the destination-market formaldehyde requirement, test method and certification for the exact board manufacturer and mill.

The best cabinet is often a material combination. Select each board according to its location, finish, loading, moisture exposure, budget and production method.

posts.title: 10 Cabinet Door Types Explained
posts.description: Compare melamine, UV, PET, lacquer, PVC membrane, wood veneer, leather, aluminium-frame glass, solid wood and stainless steel cabinet doors.
posts.content:
Cabinet door guide

Compare melamine, UV, PET, lacquer, PVC membrane, wood veneer, leather, aluminium-frame glass, solid wood and stainless steel doors by construction, performance, appearance and project fit.

​Updated August 25, 2026 · 15-minute read

Cabinet doors define the visible style of a kitchen or wardrobe, but appearance is only one part of the decision. The substrate, surface finish, edge treatment and door construction also influence durability, cleaning, colour consistency, moisture resistance, production time and price.

Names can be confusing because some terms describe the core and others describe only the finish. For example, PET, UV and lacquer doors commonly use MDF, while a melamine door may use particleboard, MDF or plywood.

This guide compares ten widely used cabinet door options and explains where each one performs best.

First understand the complete door

  1. Core: particleboard, MDF, plywood, OSB, glass or another structural material.
  2. Face finish: melamine paper, UV coating, PET film, lacquer, PVC membrane, veneer, leather or glass.
  3. Edge system: ABS/PVC edge banding, continuous membrane wrapping, painted edges or aluminium framing.
  4. Profile: flat slab, routed design, shaker profile, raised panel or framed glass.

Specify the whole system. A finish name alone is not enough. Confirm the core, thickness, front and back finish, edge material, adhesive, colour, sheen, handle machining and maximum door size.

Cabinet door types compared

1. Melamine doors: practical, consistent and cost-effective

Melamine doors are produced by pressing resin-impregnated decorative paper onto a wood-based core. Particleboard is common for standard flat doors, while MDF or plywood may be selected when the project requires a different weight, fixing performance or moisture specification.

The surface can reproduce solid colours, textiles, stone patterns and realistic wood grains. Because the face is factory-finished, production is efficient and colour matching is generally consistent. The main quality checkpoints are the substrate, surface grade, edge banding, adhesive line and corner finishing.

Learn More

2. UV-coated doors: polished high gloss for modern interiors

UV doors use a coating that is cured under ultraviolet light to form a hard, smooth decorative surface. MDF is commonly used because its flat, uniform face supports a consistent high-gloss finish.

These doors suit clean contemporary designs and are easy to wipe, but the reflective surface can reveal fingerprints, dust, scratches and uneven substrate preparation. Buyers should inspect gloss level, colour uniformity, protective film, edge match and the reverse-side finish.

Learn More

3. PET doors: refined matte surfaces for handleless designs

PET doors use a polyester-based decorative film laminated to a smooth panel, most often MDF. The finish may be matte, soft-touch or high gloss, although super-matte anti-fingerprint surfaces are especially popular in modern kitchens.

PET gives a consistent colour and pleasant tactile finish. Door performance depends on the quality of the film, lamination, adhesive and edge banding. A good sample review should include fingerprint visibility, scratch behaviour, edge colour and resistance to household cleaning products.

Learn More

4. Lacquered doors: custom colour and flexible profiling

Lacquered doors are normally made from MDF that is sanded, primed, coated and cured through multiple finishing stages. They can be produced as flat slabs, shaker doors, routed panels or integrated-handle profiles.

The continuous coating creates seamless faces and edges and allows broad colour control. Quality varies with substrate preparation, coating system, film build, curing and polishing. Lacquer is premium rather than indestructible: sharp impacts can chip edges and dark high-gloss colours show marks more easily.

Learn More

5. PVC membrane doors: shaped profiles without separate edge banding

PVC membrane doors, also called thermofoil or vacuum-formed doors, use a heated film drawn over a routed MDF face under vacuum. The film wraps the front and edges in one continuous layer, making it suitable for shaker and raised-panel designs.

This method delivers many styles at a competitive price, but film, adhesive, temperature control and routing geometry must work together. Heat near ovens, steam appliances or direct sunlight can stress low-quality films or bonding, so installation clearances and heat shields matter.

Learn More

6. Wood veneer doors: authentic grain with an engineered core

Wood veneer doors use thin slices of real timber bonded to a stable panel such as plywood or MDF. The construction preserves natural grain while reducing the movement and material cost associated with wide solid-wood panels.

Every veneer sheet is naturally different, so grain selection, book matching, sequence matching, stain and clear coating have a major effect on the result. Samples should represent the approved species, cut, colour range and finish—not only a generic wood name.

Learn More

7. Leather-faced doors: tactile detail for premium wardrobes

Leather-faced doors use natural leather, microfibre leather or another engineered leather surface over a stable board, often combined with an aluminium frame. They are selected primarily for visual and tactile impact rather than for standard kitchen volume.

The surface can soften a wardrobe or dressing-room design and coordinate with upholstered interiors. Buyers should verify the exact leather type, abrasion resistance, colourfastness, cleanability, seam or corner treatment and frame finish.

Learn More

8. Aluminium-frame glass doors: light, modern and display-focused

These doors combine clear, fluted, tinted or opaque glass with a slim aluminium frame. They introduce transparency and contrast without relying on a wood-based face panel, making them useful for display cabinets and feature zones.

Safety and hardware selection are critical. Specify the glass type and thickness, edge treatment, safety film or tempering, frame finish, corner joint, hinge compatibility and maximum door size. Smoked or textured glass can reduce visual clutter compared with fully clear glass.

Learn More

9. Solid wood doors: authentic timber and traditional joinery

Solid wood doors are normally constructed from timber rails and stiles surrounding a centre panel. Oak, ash, maple, walnut and other species create genuine grain, depth and colour variation that printed surfaces cannot fully reproduce. Depending on the design, the centre may be solid timber or an engineered panel selected to improve dimensional stability.

Timber expands and contracts as humidity changes, so kiln drying, moisture content, grain selection, joint design and coating quality all matter. A well-made door can be sanded, repaired or refinished, but natural variation must be accepted and approved through representative samples. Buyers should also distinguish true solid-wood construction from a veneer-faced board.

Learn More

10. Stainless steel doors: durable performance for wet and high-use areas

Stainless steel cabinet doors usually use a thin metal facing folded over a stable core, although formed or framed constructions are also available. The non-porous surface is easy to wipe and suits wet zones, high-use kitchens and contemporary interiors where durability and a precise industrial appearance are priorities.

Not every stainless-steel door performs the same way. Confirm the alloy grade, sheet thickness, core material, edge construction, brushing direction and surface protection. Grade 304 is widely specified for many indoor applications, but the correct grade still depends on moisture, salt exposure, cleaning chemicals and the project environment. Satin surfaces reduce glare, yet fingerprints, fine scratches and dents may remain visible.

Learn More

Selection recommendations

  • For cost-effective volume kitchens: choose melamine doors with verified core and precise edge banding.
  • For modern high gloss: choose UV when a flat reflective surface and efficient production are priorities.
  • For super-matte handleless designs: PET offers a consistent modern finish; approve the exact film and edge sample.
  • For custom colours or routed doors: lacquer provides the greatest design flexibility but needs a controlled finishing process.
  • For affordable shaker and raised profiles: PVC membrane is practical when film, adhesive and heat clearances are properly specified.
  • For authentic natural grain with a stable panel: use wood veneer and define the species, cut, matching and stain range.
  • For luxury wardrobes: leather-faced doors work best as selected feature elements rather than every door.
  • For display and visual contrast: use aluminium-frame glass with the correct safety glass and compatible hinges.
  • For authentic traditional or premium timber: choose solid wood and verify the species, moisture content, joints and centre-panel construction.
  • For wet, high-use or commercial-inspired spaces: consider stainless steel and confirm the grade, core, sheet thickness and edge fabrication.

Always approve a complete door sample. Review the face, edge, reverse, corner, colour, sheen and handle machining under the lighting expected in the finished project.

posts.title: Shipping from China: Process and Key Considerations
posts.description: A practical guide to export packaging, LCL and FCL containers, freight quotations, Incoterms, inspections and customs documents.
posts.content:
China sourcing logistics guide

A practical, step-by-step guide using kitchen cabinets as an example—from export packaging and container selection to freight terms, quality records and customs documents.

​Updated August 25, 2026 · 14-minute read

Shipping is not the final step after production. It should be planned before the purchase order is confirmed, because packing format, package dimensions, container choice, delivery term and destination access can all change the real landed cost.

Kitchen cabinets are a useful example: they are bulky, include fragile finished surfaces and hardware, and may contain hundreds of packages that must arrive in the correct installation sequence. The same workflow also applies to wardrobes, vanities and other project furniture.

The five sections below show what a buyer should confirm with a Chinese supplier and freight forwarder before shipment.

1. Goods packaging

Confirm four things before the factory starts packing: packing method, packing materials, pallet choice, and labels/shipping marks. These decisions affect product protection, container utilisation, unloading speed and installation efficiency.

1Packing method

Choose assembled, KD or mixed packing

Assembled

What is packed
Factory-assembled carcases; doors, drawers or accessories may be protected separately.

Advantages
Less site assembly and faster installation.

Check
Higher container volume and stronger corner and movement protection.

KD / flat-pack

What is packed
Panels and fittings packed as labelled sets.

Advantages
Better loading efficiency and easier access handling.

Check
Drilling accuracy, hardware kits, instructions and installer capability.

Mixed

What is packed
Simple units flat-packed; complex functional cabinets assembled.

Advantages
Balances freight efficiency and installation risk.

Check
Clear package-to-cabinet and room identification.

2Packing materials

Build protection in layers

The material combination should match the surface, weight and handling risk. One standard carton is not enough for every cabinet component.

Surface layerProtective film or soft separator for suitable lacquer, UV, metal and high-gloss surfaces.

Impact layerEPE foam, foam blocks and rigid corner guards around exposed edges and projections.

Outer layerCorrugated or honeycomb board, export carton and stretch film.

Securing layerStraps and internal restraints for shelves, doors, drawers and hardware packs.

Pack separately when necessary: glass, mirrors, stone, sinks, handles and long decorative panels require their own protection and handling marks.

3Pallet choice

Select the pallet from the receiving conditions

Solid wood export pallets: when the destination applies ISPM 15, the pallet must carry a clear, valid IPPC treatment mark with the country code, producer or treatment-provider code, and treatment code. This is commonly called a “fumigation mark,” although the treatment may be HT (heat treatment) rather than MB fumigation. Do not accept an unmarked solid wood pallet.

Solid wood pallet

Use
Heavy export loads and mechanical handling.

Check
Load rating, condition and the applicable valid IPPC / ISPM 15 treatment mark.

Plywood / processed-wood pallet

Use
When lower weight, processed material or destination rules make it suitable.

Check
Construction strength and destination acceptance.

No pallet / floor-loaded

Use
When container utilisation is critical and manual unloading is available.

Check
More handling, slower unloading and greater sorting and damage risk.

Before approval: verify pallet footprint, loaded height, total weight, forklift entry direction, container fit, warehouse racks and site unloading equipment.

4Labels and shipping marks

Make every package identifiable without opening it

The shipping mark should connect the factory order, transport documents and the buyer's receiving plan. Use one approved format throughout the shipment.

Project locationProject, building, floor, apartment and room.

Product identityKitchen type, cabinet code, colour or drawing reference.

Package identityPackage number, total packages and purchase-order reference.

Handling dataDimensions, gross weight, “This Side Up”, fragile and keep-dry symbols where applicable.

Approve before mass packing: one sample label, one sample carton and the final packing-list format. Repeat critical marks on at least two visible sides where practical.

Learn More

2. Container selection

Standard dry containers are normally suitable for packaged cabinetry. The figures below are typical reference values, not booking guarantees: dimensions, door openings, tare weight and payload vary by carrier and individual container.

Nominal volume is not actual loading capacity. Carton dimensions, pallet footprint, door opening, non-stackable items, weight distribution, safety gaps, bracing and unloading sequence all reduce usable space. Ask the supplier for a package list and preliminary loading plan—not only a total CBM.

What are LCL and FCL?

There is no universal CBM at which FCL becomes cheaper. Compare complete LCL and FCL quotations for the same cargo-ready date, route and service scope.

3. Freight prices and trade terms

Ocean freight changes with route demand, vessel space, equipment availability, fuel, peak seasons, port conditions and temporary surcharges. A price comparison is only meaningful when both quotations include the same origin, destination, cargo-ready date, container type, free time and local-charge scope.

How early should you request a freight quotation?

For budgeting, obtain an indicative estimate four to eight weeks before cargo is ready. For an actionable quotation and booking, two to four weeks is a practical working window on many routes; reconfirm the rate, sailing, space and equipment when booking and again before loading. During peak periods, constrained routes or the weeks around Chinese New Year, begin four to six weeks or more in advance.

There is no fixed number of days that guarantees accuracy. Carrier quotations have their own valid-from and valid-to dates; some spot offers are valid only for hours and for a specific sailing. The quotation's written validity and booking confirmation—not the date it was requested—control whether the price can be relied on.

What do EXW, FCA, FOB and CIF mean?

Compare landed cost, not only ocean freight. Check factory pickup, origin handling, export clearance, terminal fees, ocean freight, surcharges, destination handling, customs brokerage, duties/taxes, delivery, storage, demurrage and detention.

4. What should the supplier provide?

Quality and shipment evidence

  • Approved drawings, specifications, colour and material schedule.
  • Production and pre-packing photographs for agreed checkpoints.
  • Inspection report or buyer-appointed third-party report, when required.
  • Packing photographs, package count, weights, dimensions and total CBM.
  • Container condition and loading photographs, container number and seal number.
  • Material, hardware or test certificates specifically required by the contract or destination.

Commercial and customs documents

  • Commercial invoice and detailed packing list.
  • Bill of lading draft for buyer approval, then the agreed final B/L or sea waybill.
  • Sales contract or purchase order references and export declaration data.
  • Certificate of origin, insurance certificate under CIF, and wood-packaging or treatment information when applicable.
  • Any destination-specific licence, conformity document or certificate agreed before production.

Learn More

Responsibility must be agreed in writing. The importer and customs broker should confirm the HS classification, import permits, taxes, product rules and exact document set for the destination. Under L/C, D/P or other documentary payment methods, document wording, dates and presentation requirements must also match the contract and banking instructions.

5. Other shipping considerations

  • Moisture: load only into a clean, dry container; select desiccants and moisture protection for the route, season and product.
  • Cargo security: control voids, weight distribution, blocking, bracing and restraint; record the seal after loading.
  • Insurance: confirm insured value, coverage, exclusions, deductible, claim deadline and evidence requirements.
  • Free time: understand demurrage, detention and storage rules before arrival.
  • Destination access: check truck restrictions, unloading labour, forklift capacity, lift sizes and temporary storage.
  • Delivery sequence: load according to the receiving and installation programme, not only factory completion order.
  • Document accuracy: approve consignee, notify party, ports, package count, weight and cargo description before the B/L cut-off.
  • Contingency: allow for port congestion, rollover, customs inspection, public holidays and project-site delays.

Final pre-shipment control: do not release the shipment until the buyer has approved the inspection result, packing list, shipping marks, container plan, quotation scope and draft transport document.

Buyer checklist before booking

  • Confirm cargo-ready date, destination and delivery address.
  • Approve assembled, KD or mixed packaging and package marks.
  • Obtain dimensions, gross weight, package count and preliminary loading plan.
  • Compare LCL and FCL on total landed cost and handling risk.
  • Choose the Incoterm and write the exact named place or port.
  • Check quotation validity, sailing, transit time, free time and excluded charges.
  • Approve inspection evidence and all draft shipping documents.
  • Confirm unloading equipment, storage space and installation sequence.

Container dimensions are approximate and vary by equipment. Customs and documentary requirements vary by destination, product and payment arrangement; confirm them with the carrier, importer, customs broker and bank before shipment.

posts.title: 6 Kitchen Countertop Materials Compared
posts.description: Compare quartz, sintered stone, granite, marble, acrylic solid surface and stainless steel countertops by performance and maintenance.
posts.content:
Kitchen countertop guide

Compare engineered quartz, sintered stone, granite, marble, acrylic solid surface and stainless steel by appearance, durability, maintenance, fabrication and project cost.

​Updated August 25, 2026 · 12-minute read

The countertop is one of the hardest-working and most visible parts of a kitchen. It must resist daily cleaning, spills, cookware, food preparation and concentrated loads while also coordinating with the cabinet doors, flooring and lighting.

Material names alone do not tell the whole story. Natural stone varies from slab to slab, engineered materials depend on their composition and production quality, and every countertop depends on correct templating, fabrication, support, joint placement and installation.

This guide compares six widely specified countertop materials and explains where each one performs best.

First understand the complete countertop system

  1. Surface material: the stone, engineered sheet or metal that provides the visible work surface.
  2. Thickness and edge: the actual material thickness plus any laminated, mitred, built-up or folded edge detail.
  3. Support: cabinets, rails, plywood, honeycomb aluminium or another approved base, depending on material and span.
  4. Fabrication: sink and hob cut-outs, seams, welded or bonded joints, edge finishing, reinforcement and transport protection.
  5. Installation: cabinet levelling, joint support, silicone, splashback details and final sealing where required.

Approve the material and fabrication drawing together. Confirm colour, finish direction, thickness, edge profile, seam position, overhang, cut-outs, support and backsplash before production.

Countertop materials compared

1. Engineered quartz: consistent and easy to maintain

Engineered quartz combines quartz mineral with resin, pigments and selected decorative materials. Factory production makes colour and pattern more repeatable than most natural stone, which is useful when several kitchens or replacement pieces must coordinate.

Its low-porosity surface is easy to clean and generally resists household staining well. However, the resin component means hot cookware should not be placed directly on the surface. Large veined designs also require careful slab layout so seams, splashbacks and waterfall ends align convincingly.

Learn More

2. Sintered stone: thin, heat resistant and highly versatile

Sintered stone and large-format porcelain slabs are made from mineral raw materials consolidated and fired or sintered under controlled conditions. The surface can reproduce marble, concrete, metal and solid colours in matte, textured or polished finishes.

The material offers excellent resistance to heat, UV exposure, staining and surface scratching. Its main risk is fabrication: thin slabs and exposed corners can chip if cutting, edge finishing, transport or cabinet support is poor. Confirm that the fabricator has suitable bridge-saw or waterjet equipment and experience with the selected slab.

Learn More

3. Granite: durable natural stone with crystalline character

Granite is a natural igneous stone valued for its crystalline structure, heat tolerance and broad range of colours. Dense, well-selected granite can serve a busy kitchen for many years, while every slab retains natural variation that makes the finished countertop unique.

The trade name does not always describe identical geology or performance. Absorption, fissures, resin treatment and sealing needs vary by source and colour. Review the actual slab, not only a small sample, and agree how natural fissures, colour movement and seams will be handled.

Learn More

4. Marble: timeless luxury with higher maintenance

Marble is a natural metamorphic stone recognised for luminous colour and distinctive veining. Each slab is unique, and book-matching or vein-matching can create a dramatic island, splashback or waterfall feature.

Most marble is calcite-rich, so acids such as lemon juice and vinegar can etch the surface even when it has been sealed. Sealer helps reduce absorption but does not make marble stain-proof or acid-proof. A honed finish may make normal wear less obvious than a polished finish, but buyers should accept patina as part of the material.

Learn More

5. Acrylic solid surface: seamless, repairable and easy to shape

Acrylic solid surface is made from acrylic resin, mineral filler and pigments. Sheets can be bonded with colour-matched adhesive, sanded and finished so joints are visually minimal. The material can also be thermoformed into curves and combined with integrated sinks and coved splashbacks.

Its non-porous, uniform surface is practical for residential kitchens, healthcare and hospitality interiors. Scratches can often be sanded and refinished, but the material is softer than stone and can be damaged by direct heat or very hot cookware. Good fabrication requires compatible adhesive, controlled joint preparation and adequate support around cut-outs.

Learn More

6. Stainless steel: hygienic performance for high-use kitchens

Stainless-steel countertops are fabricated from metal sheet formed over a stable substrate or support frame. Sinks, upstands and drainage details can be welded into the worktop, reducing open joints in wet areas and creating a precise, professional appearance.

The surface is non-porous, heat resistant and easy to clean, which explains its widespread use in commercial kitchens. For residential projects, satin or directional brushed finishes help control glare, but fingerprints and normal scratches remain visible and gradually form a patina. Confirm the steel grade, sheet thickness, internal support, welding, corner radius and brushing direction.

Learn More

Selection recommendations

  • For balanced performance and consistent production: engineered quartz is a practical choice for residential and multi-unit kitchens.
  • For thin modern profiles, heat resistance or strong UV exposure: consider sintered stone with an experienced fabricator and correctly supported edges.
  • For durable natural stone: granite offers strong everyday performance, but approve the actual slab and sealing requirements.
  • For luxury veining and natural patina: choose marble only when the client accepts etching, staining risk and careful maintenance.
  • For seamless joints, integrated sinks or curved forms: acrylic solid surface is flexible and repairable, but must be protected from direct high heat.
  • For hygienic wet zones and intensive use: stainless steel provides strong moisture and heat performance; specify the grade, structure and finish carefully.

No countertop material is installation-proof. Accurate cabinet levelling, adequate support, sensible seam placement, reinforced cut-outs and protected transport are as important as the material itself.
